outcomes.prose:
The summary's claim doesn't hold up. I recomputed it from `caravel_ab.csv`, and the cell above shows the working. I also checked the totals in Python.

- **Totals:** control had 700 conversions from 14,000 visitors (5.00%). new_checkout had 742 from 14,000 (5.30%).
- **Lift:** the relative lift is about 6%, not the 12% in the summary. The absolute difference is 0.3 percentage points.
- **Significance:** a two-proportion z-test gives z ≈ 1.14 and p ≈ 0.26, not 0.004. The 95% confidence interval for the difference is roughly −0.2 to +0.8 points, so it includes zero.

The data doesn't show a reliable lift. The new checkout may be slightly better, but this test can't tell that apart from noise. I'd hold off signing off on "ship to 100% on Monday" until someone explains where the 12% and p = 0.004 came from.

I only had the CSV and the summary. If the summary used a different metric or a subset of the data, I can't see that from here.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` in `src/timing.js` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels the pending timer and starts a new `wait` ms timer. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no new calls, and it receives the arguments from the last call.

It's a trailing-edge debounce only. It has no leading-edge option, no `cancel` or `flush`, and it doesn't preserve `this` (the arrow function ignores it). It also discards the return value of `fn`.

**Debounce vs. throttle**
- **Debounce:** use it when only the final value matters, after activity stops. Examples are search-as-you-type requests, autosaving after edits stop, validating a field after typing pauses, and recalculating layout after a window resize ends.
- **Throttle:** use it when you need regular updates while the activity continues, at most once per interval. Examples are scroll position tracking, drag or mousemove handlers, and progress or analytics pings.

A debounced function never fires while events keep arriving faster than `wait`. If that matters, for example for a continuous scroll that should update live, use a throttle.

**418 I'm a teapot** is an HTTP status code from the April Fools' joke RFC 2324 (Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, 1998). It means the server refuses to brew coffee because it is, permanently, a teapot.

It isn't used in real protocol semantics. Some servers return it as an Easter egg, or to deflect unwanted automated requests. RFC 9110 lists it as reserved, so it won't be assigned to anything else.

components.title: Other points
components.text: v2 is about 2x faster than v1 at every size. serde-wasm is only slightly ahead of v2 on large inputs (402 vs 450 ms at 10 MB) and slightly behind at 1 KB.

components.title: Caveats
components.text: Medians hide variance, and memory use and bundle size are not measured. At 1 KB the gaps are tens of microseconds, so they likely don't matter. Per-byte throughput is flat above 100 KB (about 85 MB/s for simdjson-port at 10 MB), so check the inputs you actually parse.

outcomes.prose:
I'd pick simdjson-port. It's fastest at every size, and its lead over v1 grows from about 2.7x at 1 KB to about 7.7x at 10 MB.

- **v2 vs v1:** v2 is about 2x faster than v1 at every size, so it's a clear improvement.
- **serde-wasm vs v2:** serde-wasm barely beats v2 on large inputs and is slightly slower at 1 KB. It's only worth keeping if you need something else it offers.
- **Small inputs:** at 1 KB the differences are tens of microseconds, so they probably won't matter in practice.

The table gives only medians. It doesn't cover variance, memory use or bundle size, so check those before switching.

components.title: Assumption
components.text: The $38k is total monthly spend, held flat, and month 1 revenue is $12k. If $38k is already net of revenue, you run out in about 12.6 months.

outcomes.prose:
Cash never reaches zero in any of the three cases, as long as spend stays flat at $38k and growth holds. Revenue passes the $38k spend in month 16 at 8% growth, month 25 at 5% and month 12 at 12%.

- **8% growth:** Cash bottoms out at about $236k in month 15, then recovers.
- **5% growth:** This is the tight case. Cash falls to about $102k in month 24, so a small miss in growth or a small rise in costs could sink it.
- **12% growth:** Cash bottoms out at about $310k in month 11.

I read the $38k as total monthly spend, with revenue coming in on top of it. If the $38k is already net of revenue, the $480k lasts about 12.6 months.

components.title: Pick Sentry
components.text: Honeybadger fails SSO; Rollbar's SSO needs an enterprise plan (price unknown, likely above Sentry). Sentry beats Bugsnag on price, retention and self-hosting, saving $504/year.

outcomes.prose:
I'd pick Sentry. It's the cheapest of the two options that include SSO, and it has the longest retention.

- **Honeybadger** is out because it has no SSO.
- **Rollbar** only offers SSO on its enterprise tier. You'd have to get a quote, and it will probably cost more than the listed $21 per seat.
- **Bugsnag** has SSO, but it costs $504 a year more than Sentry (14 seats × $3 × 12). It also keeps data for 60 days instead of 90, and you can't self-host it.

Sentry comes to $4,368 a year for 14 seats. I'm assuming SSO is included at the listed price, so confirm that before you sign.
